newsitem.title: USA: NY governor reviews proposals to curb Swiss banks.
newsitem.headline: NY governor reviews proposals to curb Swiss banks.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki is studying proposals to curb the activities of Swiss banks to pressure them to reach a settlement with the victims of the Holocaust, a spokesman for the governor said Wednesday.

Patrick McCarthy, a spokesman for Pataki said: "He is reviewing proposals on this issue from the Assembly as well as the (New York) City Council, and he's instructed the state Banking Department to see what can be done."
McCarthy said the governor had not set a deadline for reaching a decision on the proposed curbs.
The spokesman also said Pataki was closely following the U.S. Senate Banking Committee investigations related to the issue and was committed to seeing restitution is made.
The Senate investigations are led by Senator Al D'Amato, a New York Republican who has championed the cause of the Holocaust victims.
The head of the New York State Assembly earlier announced hearings to determine "under what circumstances may a foreign bank's license or certification be revoked."

A spokesman for the state comptroller, H. Carl McCall, said that his office was aiding the survivors of the Holocaust by helping to track bank accounts. He added the state did not appear to own any stock of Swiss banks in its pension funds, though information still was being gathered.

"We're trying to find out as much as we can about what type of dealings we have with them, what type of any wrongdoing was commited," said Dennis Tompkins, a spokesman for McCall, saying any further response was premature.
The New York City Council Speaker proposed a bill that would stop the city from depositing money in Swiss banks until the Swiss government set up a compensation fund for Holocaust victims.

The council speaker, Peter Vallone -- saying the city was the financial capital of the world -- also proposed stiffer actions if a satisfactory agreement between the Swiss government and Jewish groups was not reached.

"We will follow the same course that we did with South Africa," he told Reuters television in an interview. "We were the first ones, which not only prevented deposits (but) divested our pension monies and prevented corporations that did business with the City of New York from investing in South Africa."

The city comptroller, Alan Hevesi, in prepared remarks, appeared to hint that he would be willing to support a modified version of the council's bill, offering his office's resources to ensure that the bill "finally adopted" would be as effective as possible.

New York City as of January 29 had about $4.5 billion in cash, of which $225 million was invested with Credit Suisse Group, a spokesman for Hevesi said, noting that the amount of cash the city has invested fluctuates sharply.

The city's pensions own stock in three Swiss banks: 262,800 shares of Credit Suisse Group, which were worth almost $26 million, 56,700 shares of Swiss Bank Corp, which were valued at $10.8 million, and 22,800 shares of Union Bank, pegged at about $13.3 million, he added.
